title: Windsurf vs Cursor vs Claude Code (2026): 3-Way Showdown

blocks.text: Windsurf vs Cursor vs Claude Code (2026): 3-Way Showdown

Windsurf (now Devin Desktop), Cursor and Claude Code compared for 2026: agent-first IDE vs model-flexible IDE vs terminal agent, with current prices from each vendor's own pricing page and a clear pick for each team type.

TL;DR

Windsurf (renamed Devin Desktop by its owner Cognition on June 2, 2026) is the best pick if you want an IDE that drives itself: an agent-first editor where Devin Local, the successor to Cascade, plans across files and runs commands, and a Kanban command center manages local and cloud agents.

Cursor is the best pick if you want a familiar editor with a wide model menu: Cursor's docs say it "supports frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceXAI, and more," with Agent, cloud agents and a CLI.
Claude Code is the best pick if you want headless, scriptable agentic engineering: terminal-native, with subagents, MCP servers, hooks, print mode for scripts and CI, and GitHub Actions support.
All three are good. The right one depends on whether you want an IDE that runs agents, an IDE with an agent, or an agent that happens to also write code.
Checked September 26, 2026 against each vendor's own pricing page.

By 2026, the conversation has stopped being "should we use AI to code?" and started being "which agent stack do we standardize on?" Windsurf, Cursor, and Claude Code are three serious contenders for engineering teams that ship to production. Each one has a different center of gravity. Windsurf is built around the IDE-as-agent, Cursor around the IDE-as-AI-cockpit, and Claude Code around the terminal-as-control-plane.

One thing changed since this guide first ran. Windsurf is no longer an independent Codeium product. OpenAI's planned $3 billion acquisition fell apart on July 11, 2025 (TechCrunch), Google paid $2.4 billion to license the technology and hire the CEO and top researchers, and Cognition, the maker of Devin, signed a definitive agreement to acquire Windsurf on July 14, 2025 (Cognition). On June 2, 2026, Cognition renamed the editor to Devin Desktop (Devin blog), and windsurf.com now redirects to devin.ai. We keep the Windsurf name in this guide because most people still search for it.

The hard part is that marketing pages make these tools sound identical. They all say "agentic," "multi-file," "context-aware," and "fast." The comparison that matters is what each tool does when you stop typing: a payment refactor in a Next.js app, a Postgres migration with downstream code rewrites, a flaky test triage across 40 files. This guide describes each tool from its own docs and pricing pages. It is not a benchmark and we did not time or score the tools against each other.

It compares Windsurf, Cursor, and Claude Code across the dimensions that decide adoption: surface, agentic depth, multi-file refactor, multi-model support, pricing, and ecosystem. Honest pros and cons, and a framework at the end so you can pick the right one for your team rather than the one with the loudest changelog.

Windsurf deep dive

Windsurf is now Devin Desktop, Cognition's agent-first IDE. It started at Codeium as an editor where the agent (Cascade) was the primary way you worked, not a sidebar. After the Cognition acquisition, the June 2026 rename turned it into what Cognition calls "the command center for managing all your agents in one place."

The agent is still the differentiator, but it changed. Cognition says "Devin Local is the successor to Cascade as our primary local agent," that it is "up to 30% more token efficient," and that it "supports modern features like subagents." The legacy Cascade agent was available through July 1. You describe what you want, the agent plans, edits across files and runs commands, and every local and cloud agent shows up in a single Kanban view. Your plan, pricing, extensions and settings carried over in the update.

The trade-off is that Windsurf is most powerful when you stay inside it. Its core loop is bound to the desktop app. Cognition sells a separate Devin CLI and Devin Cloud for terminal and cloud work, so running agents headlessly means adopting more of the Devin stack, not scripting the editor itself. If your workflow is "open IDE → ship feature → close IDE," Windsurf is a strong fit. If your workflow is "agent runs in a GitHub Action and opens a PR," the editor is not the right shape on its own.
Strengths
An agent-first editor: Devin Local does the multi-file work, and the Kanban command center tracks every running agent
Runs other agents too: the Agent Client Protocol lets Codex, Claude Agent and OpenCode sit next to Devin
Extensions, MCP servers and settings carried over from Windsurf automatically
Enterprise plan lists SAML/OIDC SSO, enterprise controls and a dedicated deployment option
Limitations
The product is mid-transition: new name, new default agent, and Cascade retired in July 2026, so older tutorials and configs may not match what you see
The editor itself is not a headless tool; CI and scripted runs go through Cognition's separate Devin CLI or cloud products
Cursor deep dive
Cursor is an AI-native IDE built by Anysphere. Its core idea is to keep an editor engineers already know and rebuild the AI surface so it is fast, multi-model, and useful for non-trivial edits.

In 2026, Cursor's selling point is breadth. Its docs list models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google along with others, and Cursor ships its own Composer models, so you can run one model for a quick edit and another for a reasoning-heavy refactor without leaving the editor. Agent runs multi-step tasks, cloud agents and automations run work in the background, and Bugbot reviews code. Cursor also has a CLI with a print mode its docs describe as built "for non-interactive scenarios like scripts, CI pipelines, or automation."

The trade-off is that Cursor is still an IDE first. It is excellent at "edit these files together," "write this function with full repo context," and "explain this stack trace." For "run for 20 minutes, fix the failing CI, open a PR, and update the changelog," the CLI and cloud agents can do the job, but teams that want hooks, subagents and MCP wired into scripts as the main way of working tend to reach for Claude Code. Cursor is an IDE that has an agent. Claude Code is an agent that happens to also work in your IDE.
Strengths
One of the widest model menus in any IDE: pick the right model per task
Familiar editor surface and low onboarding cost
Agent, cloud agents and Bugbot cover edits, background work and review
MCPs, skills and hooks on the Individual plan, and a team marketplace for shared rules and plugins on Teams
Limitations
The CLI exists, but the product is built around the editor; headless use is a secondary surface
The "best model for this task" decision still falls on you; flexibility costs cognitive overhead
Claude Code deep dive

Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool, and its shape differs from Windsurf and Cursor: it started in the terminal. Anthropic's docs describe it as a tool that "reads your codebase, edits files, runs commands, and integrates with your development tools," available in the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app and the browser.

In a Claude Code session, the lead agent can spawn subagents to research files, run tests, or execute scoped tasks in parallel. It connects to MCP servers (databases, browsers, third-party APIs, internal tools) as data sources. Hooks run shell commands before or after Claude Code actions, like auto-formatting after every edit or running lint before a commit. And because it is CLI-native, claude -p runs it non-interactively in scripts, and Anthropic documents GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD setups for automated review and triage.

The trade-off is the on-ramp. If your team has lived in an IDE for a decade and treats the terminal as a deploy console, Claude Code's "agent-first, IDE-second" stance feels backwards at first. The payoff comes when you use it for work that does not fit into a single IDE session: long refactors, scheduled jobs, automated PR review, agent swarms. That is where the architecture compounds.
Strengths
Deepest set of agent building blocks of the three: subagents, MCP, hooks, headless mode, scheduled routines and the Agent SDK
Terminal-native means it composes with CI, scripts, other agents and queues
The same CLAUDE.md files, settings and MCP servers work across terminal, IDE, desktop and web
Included in paid Claude plans, so a Pro seat covers light use without API billing
Limitations
CLI-first surface has a learning curve for engineers who live in the IDE
Runs Anthropic's Claude models only: no multi-provider routing in the core experience
Head-to-head
Surface

Windsurf and Cursor are both desktop IDEs: familiar editor, sidebar, tabs, terminal. The difference is what the AI surface feels like. In Cursor, the AI is a panel and a command palette. In Windsurf (Devin Desktop), the AI is the workflow, with a board of running agents as the default screen. Claude Code started in the terminal and now also runs as a VS Code extension (including in Cursor), a JetBrains plugin, a desktop app and on the web.
Pick by where you want to spend the most time. If that is the editor, choose Cursor or Windsurf. If that is the shell, choose Claude Code.
Agentic depth
This is where the three diverge most.
Windsurf (Devin Local): strong on coherence inside the editor, with subagents and a board that tracks local and cloud agents. Great for in-session features.
Cursor (Agent, cloud agents, CLI): strong on flexibility. Pick the model, scope the task, run it locally or in the cloud.
Claude Code: strongest on building blocks. Subagents, MCP, hooks, headless print mode, routines. Built for runs that outlast a single session.
For a 30-minute feature ticket, all three work. For a 4-hour overnight refactor with self-review, Claude Code's headless mode, hooks and scheduled routines are the most direct fit.
Multi-file refactor

Multi-file is table stakes in 2026. Cursor's Agent handles tightly scoped edits across a handful of files. Windsurf's agent works inside one editor session and keeps the change in view. Claude Code, with subagents, can fan out: one agent renames the API, another updates the tests, a third updates the docs, and the lead agent reconciles.
For routine refactors, Cursor and Windsurf are excellent. For larger ones (schema migrations with downstream code changes, API renames across a monorepo), Claude Code's architecture is the safer bet.
Multi-model

Cursor and Windsurf both offer a model menu now. Cursor's docs list frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceXAI and more, plus its own Composer models. Devin's Pro plan lists frontier models from OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, SpaceXAI and open source, plus Cognition's SWE-2. Claude Code runs Anthropic's Claude models only: a feature for teams standardizing on Claude, a constraint for teams that want provider flexibility.
If your reality is "we use the best model per task and we want one UI," Cursor is the answer, with Windsurf close behind.
Pricing
Prices below come from each vendor's own pricing page on September 26, 2026.

Claude Code can also be billed per token through the Anthropic API. Anthropic's cost docs say that across enterprise deployments the average is "around $13 per developer per active day and $150-250 per developer per month," with 90% of users under $30 per active day. Heavy agent runs can cost more than a flat IDE subscription. For most teams, the deciding factor is not list price but how much engineer time the tool saves each week.
For a deeper Cursor vs Claude Code breakdown, see our Cursor vs Claude Code comparison.
Ecosystem

Cursor has MCPs, skills and hooks on the Individual plan, and a team marketplace for internal rules, skills and plugins on Teams. Its large user base means many shared prompts, configs and rules files.

Windsurf now sits inside Cognition's Devin stack: Devin Desktop, Devin Local, Devin Cloud and Devin CLI. Extensions and MCP servers carried over from Windsurf, and the Agent Client Protocol lets you run other agents in the same app.

Claude Code is built for composition. MCP is an open standard for connecting AI tools to external data, Claude Code supports it natively, and the Agent SDK lets you build your own agents on Claude Code's tools. If you are building an internal agent platform, this is the base layer.

When to pick each

Pick Windsurf if your team wants the cleanest IDE-driven agent experience. You ship features inside the editor, you want fewer prompts and more flow, you like seeing every running agent on one board, and headless / CI agent runs are not your primary use case. Plan for the Devin Desktop rename: your seats, docs and onboarding will say Devin now.

Pick Cursor if your team wants a familiar editor with a wide model menu. You want to route tasks to different frontier models, your engineers want near-zero retraining, and you want a large community to learn from. Strong fit for AI-native startups, multi-model shops, and teams that value flexibility over depth.

Pick Claude Code if your team is serious about agentic engineering as a discipline, not a feature. You want subagents, MCP servers, hooks, headless runs, CI integration, and the ability to compose agents into larger systems. Strong fit for platform teams, internal-tools teams, and any org standardizing on Claude. If you want help designing or implementing a Claude-native agent stack, our Claude Code agency practice does exactly that.

For most teams, the right move in 2026 is to standardize on one as the daily driver and keep a second for the workflows where it is the better tool. Cursor + Claude Code is a common pairing. Windsurf + Claude Code works equally well. The combination that does not work is "all three, all the time": that is just context-switching tax.

FAQ
What is the difference between Windsurf and Cursor?

Both are AI-first desktop IDEs. Cursor leans on multi-model flexibility (pick OpenAI, Anthropic, Google or Cursor's own Composer models per task) and a familiar editor experience. Windsurf, now Devin Desktop, leans on an agent-first workflow where Devin Local drives multi-file edits and terminal commands and a board tracks every agent. Cursor is broader; Windsurf is deeper inside the IDE.
Is Claude Code an IDE?

No. Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool. It started in the terminal and now also runs as VS Code and JetBrains extensions, a desktop app and on the web, and it exposes subagents, MCP servers and hooks. Think of it as an agent that happens to write code, rather than an IDE that happens to host an agent.
Can I use Claude Code with Cursor or Windsurf?

Yes, and many teams do. Claude Code runs in any terminal, including the integrated terminals inside Cursor and Windsurf, and Anthropic's docs link a Claude Code extension install for Cursor. Devin Desktop can also run a Claude agent through the Agent Client Protocol. A common pattern is editor work in Cursor or Windsurf and longer runs, CI jobs and MCP-heavy work in Claude Code.
Which is best for large refactors?

Claude Code, in most cases. Subagents let you fan out work across an API rename, the tests, and the docs in parallel, then reconcile, and headless mode lets the run continue in CI. Windsurf's Devin Local keeps a change coherent inside one editor session. Cursor's Agent is excellent for tightly scoped multi-file edits.
Which has the best multi-model support?

Cursor, with Windsurf close behind. Cursor's docs list frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceXAI and more, plus its own Composer models. Devin's Pro plan lists OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, SpaceXAI and open-source models plus SWE-2. Claude Code runs Anthropic's Claude models only: a strength if you are standardizing on Claude and a limitation if you want provider flexibility.
How much do they cost in 2026?

Cursor and Windsurf (Devin Desktop) have free tiers; Claude's Free plan does not include Claude Code. Cursor Individual starts at $20/month, Devin Pro is $20/month, and Claude Pro with Claude Code is $20/month billed monthly or $17/month billed annually. Team seats run $40 (Cursor), $40 plus an $80 base (Devin) and $20 to $125 (Claude). Enterprise pricing is custom or seat plus usage.
Should we standardize on one tool?

For default workflows, yes: context-switching across 3 agent stacks is a tax. Most teams pick one as the daily driver and keep a second for the cases where it is clearly the better tool (Claude Code for headless and CI runs, Cursor or Windsurf for editor-first work). What does not work is "all three, all the time."
Where do we start if we have never used any of them?

Try Cursor first if your team lives in a VS Code-style editor: the on-ramp is the gentlest. Try Windsurf if you want the agent to feel like the primary workflow, not a side panel. Try Claude Code if you already think in terms of agents, pipelines, and automation. For a stack designed end-to-end around Claude, our Claude Code agency team can architect it with you. Standardizing on Cursor instead? Our Cursor development agency wires it into your actual repo and CI, not just a solo trial.
Who owns Windsurf now?

Cognition, the company behind the Devin coding agent. Cognition signed a definitive agreement to acquire Windsurf on July 14, 2025, days after OpenAI's planned $3 billion deal fell apart and Google licensed the technology and hired Windsurf's CEO. On June 2, 2026, Cognition renamed the Windsurf editor to Devin Desktop, and windsurf.com now redirects to devin.ai.
Is Cascade still available in Windsurf?

No, not as the main agent. Cognition's June 2, 2026 announcement says Devin Local is the successor to Cascade as the primary local agent, and the legacy Cascade agent stayed available through July 1. Devin Local supports subagents, and Cognition says it is up to 30% more token efficient. Old Cascade tutorials still describe the general flow, but menus and names have changed.
Can Cursor run headless in CI like Claude Code?

Yes, for basic cases. Cursor's CLI docs describe a print mode for "non-interactive scenarios like scripts, CI pipelines, or automation." Claude Code has the same pattern with claude -p, plus documented GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD setups, hooks and scheduled routines. If CI automation is your main use, compare both CLIs on one real pipeline before you standardize.
